title: The Grand Opening

jokes.text: Hank reads the applause sign wrong on purpose: 'That sign says applesauce. No, no. I'm kidding. It says applause.'
jokes.setup: Hank is warming up the studio audience and draws their attention to the applause sign
jokes.punchline: He pretends it says 'applesauce' before correcting himself — a deliberate low-stakes dad-joke that immediately establishes Hank's eager-to-please, slightly desperate warmup personality
jokes.explanation: A mildly amusing bit that works primarily as character comedy — the joke itself is weak but the fact that THIS is Hank's idea of crowd-warming material is the real gag. Establishes his blowhard-mediocre energy immediately.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Now that sign Says 'applesauce.' No, no. I'm kidding. It says 'applause.'

jokes.text: Martin Mull on air: 'I know how much this show means to Larry and what a stickler he is for quality. At least, to the extent that one can have any in television.'
jokes.setup: Martin Mull opens his guest hosting stint with apparent flattery of Larry Sanders and the show
jokes.punchline: He undercuts the compliment with a bleak industry-wide dig at television's inherent lack of quality — delivered with breezy self-awareness
jokes.explanation: Sharp meta-commentary on the medium delivered in character. The joke is insider-smart — it doesn't punch at a specific target but at the whole enterprise of TV itself, which is rich coming from a man sitting in the host's chair. Good economy and the deadpan delivery implied by Mull's persona elevates it.

dialogue.speaker: Martin Mull
dialogue.line: This is really very, very Close to a thrill for me.

jokes.text: Martin Mull: 'Well, thank gosh for commercials. We'll be right back.' — ending his opening remarks abruptly after one joke
jokes.setup: Martin Mull is clearly nervous and has just made a mildly self-deprecating remark about TV quality
jokes.punchline: Rather than push through, he immediately bails to commercial with 'thank gosh for commercials' — hilariously surrendering mid-monologue
jokes.explanation: Beautiful economy — the joke is in the retreat itself, the acknowledgment that he has nothing and isn't going to pretend otherwise. Very Larry Sanders Show in spirit: the anti-performance is funnier than any monologue joke could be.

dialogue.speaker: Martin Mull
dialogue.line: I know how much This show means to Larry And what a stickler He is for quality. At least, to the extent That one can have any In television.

jokes.text: Martin Mull backstage: 'I can't believe I was actually nervous out there. I used to do this shit in my sleep.'
jokes.setup: Mull has just made a stumbling, barely-functional on-air appearance
jokes.punchline: He claims he 'used to do this in his sleep,' implying past competence — which we have no evidence of and the audience has just watched him barely survive two minutes
jokes.explanation: Light irony that works because we've just watched the evidence contradict the claim. Functional observational comedy about showbiz self-delusion, but not sharpened to a real point.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: I've been burning the, Uh, bulb at both ends

jokes.text: Hank: 'I've been burning the, uh, bulb at both ends, that's all.' — mangling 'burning the candle at both ends'
jokes.setup: Martin Mull notes Hank looks tired; Hank reaches for an idiom to explain his exhaustion
jokes.punchline: He swaps 'candle' for 'bulb,' producing a malapropism that reveals both his exhausted brain and his fundamental linguistic sloppiness
jokes.explanation: Delightfully specific character work — 'bulb' is close enough to be a plausible brain-fart but wrong enough to be absurd. Could only come from Hank, who is always slightly off. High character integration because it captures his intellectually lazy-but-confident personality. Passes by quickly which adds to its charm.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: That's not the question. What are you gonna Do this weekend?

jokes.text: Hank hijacks his own on-air segment to plug his restaurant, inviting Martin Mull to the 'Grand Opening of Hank's Look-Around Cafe, Friday night. Hank Kingsley, Proprietor.'
jokes.setup: Martin Mull asks Hank what he's doing this weekend as a soft on-air transition
jokes.punchline: Hank seizes the entire segment to do a full promotional plug for his restaurant, complete with address, and even holds up what appears to be a menu or card for the camera
jokes.explanation: Peak Hank energy — the total lack of self-awareness in weaponizing a live broadcast for personal commercial gain is perfectly in character. The formality of 'Hank Kingsley, Proprietor' is the detail that elevates it. High character integration: this is something only Hank would do, and the show has set up exactly this kind of breach of professional norms.

dialogue.speaker: Martin Mull
dialogue.line: Nothing really Aids digestion Quite like Centrifugal force.

jokes.text: Martin Mull on the rotating floor: 'I've always been one to say, at least for my money, that nothing really aids digestion quite like centrifugal force.'
jokes.setup: Hank confirms the restaurant has a spinning floor; Mull obliges with an on-air reaction
jokes.punchline: The mock-sage delivery of 'centrifugal force aids digestion' — stated as received wisdom — is beautifully dry and absurdist
jokes.explanation: Strong joke. The phrase 'at least for my money' mimics the cadence of genuine folk wisdom, which makes the absurdist pivot to 'centrifugal force' land harder. It's a great line reading moment and highly quotable. The joke pokes at the fundamental ridiculousness of a rotating restaurant — which the whole episode is really about — from a fresh angle.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: You're A guest host, Guest being the, uh, Operative word here.

jokes.text: Hank corners Martin Mull backstage after the segment to complain that the restaurant jokes were 'joking' — but then demands Martin clear all future 'humorous ad libs' with him first
jokes.setup: Hank insists he knows the jokes about his restaurant were just friendly ribbing
jokes.punchline: In the same breath he institutes an approval process for all future jokes, completely undermining his claim that he's relaxed about it — the self-contradiction is the joke
jokes.explanation: Classic Hank self-deception comedy — he insists he has no ego problem while demonstrating a catastrophic ego problem in real time. The 'chain of command' speech (Larry, then me, then Artie, then everyone else) is a beautiful escalation of his delusion. High character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Martin Mull
dialogue.line: You know what, I think This might fit Nicely up your ass.

jokes.text: Hank immediately follows Mull's 'up your ass' line with cheerful sincerity: 'All right. Other than that, it's just a great show!'
jokes.setup: Martin Mull has just insulted Hank directly.
jokes.punchline: Hank pivots instantly to enthusiastic professional positivity — the gap between the insult and his breezy response reveals his total emotional compartmentalization (and obliviousness).
jokes.explanation: The laugh is entirely in the tonal whiplash. Hank doesn't process the insult — he just moves on, which is both funnier and more revealing than any comeback. This is pure character comedy: only Hank's particular brand of narcissistic insulation produces this response. Strong economy, character integration is near-perfect.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: They're reddish-brown, And they-- It completely, um-- It clashes with-- Clashes with The banquette.

jokes.text: Martin Mull's exit line to Hank: 'You know what, I think this might fit nicely up your ass.' — then cheerfully pivots: 'All right. Other than that, it's just a great show!'
jokes.setup: Hank has just told Martin he must pre-clear all future ad libs; Martin absorbs this patiently
jokes.punchline: Martin delivers a precise, undramatic threat, then immediately re-establishes sunny professional warmth — the tonal whiplash is the joke
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. The two-beat structure is perfect: the measured, almost forensic delivery of the threat ('I think this might fit nicely up your ass') followed by the instant sunny pivot ('Other than that, it's just a great show!') is textbook economy and tonal misdirection. It's exactly what a professional entertainer would say — the insult packaged inside a compliment. Highly quotable and earns its 8+ because of structural precision and perfect economy.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: You put him in the genuine Article, and he locks

jokes.text: Hank defends Martin Mull quitting by saying he 'was fine on that make-believe talk show, that Fernwood thing, but you put him in the genuine article and he locks'
jokes.setup: Artie confronts Hank about driving Mull to quit
jokes.punchline: Hank dismisses Mull by condescending about 'Fernwood 2-Night' (a legendary satirical talk show) as a 'make-believe' show — while he himself co-hosts a fictional talk show. The irony is total.
jokes.explanation: Rich industry-insider comedy. Hank calling 'Fernwood 2-Night' a 'make-believe talk show' while sitting on 'The Larry Sanders Show' (itself fictional) is a layered, self-aware joke. It rewards viewers who know Fernwood. The condescension is perfectly Hank: wrong and unaware. High character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: No friday night, No next night! No friday night, No next night!

jokes.text: Artie arrives to find Hank has been sleeping in the office; Hank is found amid fabric swatches for napkins at 9:30 AM
jokes.setup: Artie arrives at work to a slammed door and Hank's dramatic 'Here I am!'
jokes.punchline: Hank has been sleeping at the office, obsessively agonizing over napkin colors clashing with the banquette — the scale mismatch between his anxiety and his problem is absurd
jokes.explanation: Strong character comedy — Hank sleeping at the office surrounded by napkin swatches is a great physical situation. The mundane detail (reddish-brown napkins clashing with the banquette) buried in his exhausted rambling captures the absurd specificity of someone who has lost perspective entirely.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Did I say Jerry van dyke? I mean joan van ark.

jokes.text: Hank attempts to bribe Artie with '2 tickets to the grand opening of Hank's Look-Around Cafe, [French accent] absolutely no charge' — after Artie has just berated him
jokes.setup: Artie is furious at Hank for driving off a guest host
jokes.punchline: Hank produces grand opening tickets with a spontaneous fake French accent, as if free tickets to his own restaurant is adequate compensation for the professional chaos he's caused
jokes.explanation: The French accent is a perfect random detail — it suggests Hank has imagined this pitch before in the mirror, rehearsed the 'no charge' line with continental flair. The absurdist specificity of the accent elevates what would otherwise be a simple deflection joke.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: All my celebrity friends-- And they're just sitting In all these booths, And I get to say To them, 'hey. Hey! This one's on me,' To some of them.

jokes.text: Artie's flat response to Hank's grand opening tickets: 'It's this Friday night?' — 'I've got plans.'
jokes.setup: Hank has just offered Artie free tickets to the grand opening with great ceremony
jokes.punchline: Artie's single-line deflection — 'I've got plans' — delivered without malice or explanation, is a masterclass in comic economy
jokes.explanation: Artie's 'I've got plans' is the perfect Rip Torn deadpan beat — no explanation, no apology, no drama. The character integration is high because Artie doesn't perform emotion or manage Hank; he simply states facts. This lands because it's the first time Artie's private feelings about the restaurant are revealed, and they're devastating in their indifference.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Larry's on vacation! He's not To be disturbed.

jokes.text: The escalating history of grand opening postponements: wrong motor for rotating floor, then burst water pipe rusting the bearing for the rotating floor — each failure more specific and more absurd
jokes.setup: Phil points out the grand opening was announced months ago and never happened
jokes.punchline: Hank recounts a chain of mechanically specific disasters — each one about the rotating floor specifically — that reads as both pathetic and cosmically opposed
jokes.explanation: The joke is in the specificity: it's always the rotating floor. The universe keeps telling Hank his restaurant concept is wrong and he keeps repairing the rotating floor instead of reconsidering the concept. The escalating list structure works well here.

dialogue.speaker: Burt Reynolds
dialogue.line: No, actually I don't Live in the big house. I... I live back there in The guesthouse, you see. 'Cause I can't Afford the big house Because of the--

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Yeah, is it that thing You're going through? Divorce.

jokes.text: Hank: 'Like I've never laughed at your lame monologue jokes which I don't even get!'
jokes.setup: Hank is raging at the staff for not committing to his grand opening.
jokes.punchline: In his tantrum, Hank accidentally confesses that he laughs performatively at Larry's jokes without understanding them — revealing both his phoniness and his resentment in a single sentence.
jokes.explanation: This is one of the episode's best lines and one of the best Hank lines in the series. It's a self-own delivered as an accusation — Hank thinks he's arguing for loyalty but accidentally exposes that his entire professional persona (the loyal sidekick laughing at the host's jokes) is a performance he doesn't even understand. The 'which I don't even get' is devastating because it's so honest and so unaware. Exceptional character integration — this could only be Hank. Genuinely earns the 8+ score.

dialogue.speaker: Burt Reynolds
dialogue.line: What does it pay?

jokes.text: Hank's 'No Friday Night, No Next Night' table-rap speech, culminating in breaking something plastic
jokes.setup: Staff suggest they'll come 'the next night' instead of the Friday opening; Hank attempts to explain the logic of opening night economics
jokes.punchline: His explanation devolves into a repetitive, increasingly manic chant — 'No friday night, no next night!' — punctuated by rapping the table until something breaks
jokes.explanation: Excellent escalation comedy. The speech starts as a reasonable explanation, tips into obsessive repetition, and lands with accidental destruction — a perfect comic arc. The fact that 'No Friday Night, No Next Night' is actually logically sound but delivered with the intensity of a manifesto is what makes it funny. The plastic breaking is perfectly timed slapstick. High character integration — this is Hank at maximum.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: 3 times, I heard.

dialogue.speaker: Burt Reynolds
dialogue.line: I've been divorced 4 times.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: 4 times?

dialogue.speaker: Burt Reynolds
dialogue.line: Yeah. Who gives a shit?

jokes.text: After Hank's meltdown, Artie's assistant announces: 'The napkin people on line 4' — Artie then says: 'Get me the Jerry van Dyke file.' then immediately corrects: 'Did I say Jerry van Dyke? I mean Joan van Ark.'
jokes.setup: Artie is scrambling to find a replacement guest host after the Martin Mull disaster
jokes.punchline: The guest host search has reached Jerry van Dyke before Artie catches himself — the implied level of desperation is the joke; then correcting to Joan van Ark doesn't help
jokes.explanation: Sharp industry-insider joke that rewards savvy viewers. Jerry van Dyke was a real cultural shorthand for 'last resort casting' (known for My Mother the Car, TV's biggest flop). Catching himself mid-order and pivoting to Joan van Ark doesn't fix anything — both names signal the same level of desperation. The self-correction is the escalation. Artie's flat delivery selling this as routine crisis management is perfect.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: You do.

jokes.text: Hank: 'Artie, I need to talk to you mano a mano.' Artie: 'No.' Hank: 'Yeah, come on, sit down.' Artie: 'No!'
jokes.setup: Hank attempts to initiate a heart-to-heart with Artie using the idiom 'mano a mano'
jokes.punchline: Artie's immediate, unvarnished 'No' — repeated with escalating firmness — refuses even the premise of the conversation
jokes.explanation: Perfect two-word punch: Artie's refusal to even negotiate the terms of the conversation. The escalation from 'No.' to 'No!' when Hank pushes is elegant. Rip Torn's character is so established that the word 'No' alone delivers an entire relationship history. Maximally economical.

dialogue.speaker: Burt Reynolds
dialogue.line: Course, If you're a smoker, You'd have to smoke And then stop And then light up Again when you came In your section.

jokes.text: Hank's reverie about his celebrity friends in booths: 'Hey, hey! This one's on me — to some of them.'
jokes.setup: Hank is describing his vision for the restaurant — all his celebrity friends sitting in booths
jokes.punchline: The grandiose fantasy of generosity collapses with 'to some of them' — a tiny qualifier that reveals his actual stinginess even in his own fantasy
jokes.explanation: One of the best lines in the episode. In three words — 'to some of them' — the writers reveal everything about Hank's character: he fantasizes about generosity but can't commit even in imagination. The setup is sincere and warm, which makes the qualifier land as a genuine surprise. High originality because the joke lives in the gap between aspiration and instinct. Perfect economy, high quotability, strong character integration. Comparable in quality to the 8.0 anchor — the specificity of 'some of them' in a fantasy of largesse is genuinely clever writing.

dialogue.speaker: Burt Reynolds
dialogue.line: Like, uh, smokey and the bandit. That was a-- That was a great idea. And, uh, cannonball run. That was a-- That was a great idea.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: [Snobby voice] Ooh. Bravo.

jokes.text: Larry recruits Burt Reynolds as emergency guest host — discovers Burt lives in the guesthouse behind the big house he can't afford due to his divorce
jokes.setup: Larry runs into Burt Reynolds next door while on vacation — Burt says he 'doesn't live in the big house'
jokes.punchline: Burt lives in the guesthouse because he can't afford the main house due to his divorce — a sad, specific, celebrity humiliation played as casual small talk
jokes.explanation: Celebrity humiliation played straight — Burt Reynolds reduced to a guesthouse due to divorce is funny because it's delivered so matter-of-factly. The Larry Sanders Show specializes in this: the famous being pathetic in very human ways. The setup plays like genuine neighborly small talk before the reveal lands.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: It's beginning to smell Like a goddamn locker room.

jokes.text: Burt Reynolds's first question about guest hosting: 'What does it pay?'
jokes.setup: Larry awkwardly asks a visibly struggling Burt Reynolds if he'd want to guest host the show as a favor
jokes.punchline: Burt's immediate, unsentimental 'What does it pay?' — followed by an audience laugh cut — reveals how far his financial situation has fallen and how little goodwill remains
jokes.explanation: Exceptional economy joke. Four words that simultaneously reveal character (Burt's financial desperation), undercut the sentimentality of the moment (Larry's awkward pity ask), and function as a perfect punchline. The setup builds sympathy for Burt, making the mercenary response both funnier and sadder. Highly quotable, one of the episode's best beats.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Oh, boy, Another ego trip. Yeah. Give a guy A couple of car chases, And all of a sudden He thinks he's An incredible wit.

jokes.text: Burt Reynolds recounting his divorces; Larry says 'I've been there. Oh yeah? 3 times, I heard.' Burt: 'I've been divorced 4 times.' Larry: '4 times? Yeah. Who gives a shit?'
jokes.setup: Larry tries to bond with Burt over divorce; Burt corrects the rumored number upward to four
jokes.punchline: Larry's 'Who gives a shit?' — asked rhetorically, answered immediately by himself: 'You do' — is a perfectly constructed mini-exchange that acknowledges the subject while dismissing it
jokes.explanation: The 'who gives a shit? / you do.' exchange is elegantly structured — Larry's deflection is immediately caught and redirected by the straight man (Burt or Artie). Dark comedy about celebrity marriages treated as unremarkable statistics. Good economy and structure.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: My restaurant, At this moment, Has a very specific odor That is not conducive To the art Of fine dining...

jokes.text: Hank takes a phone call with the alcohol permit office mid-taping, putting the licensing bureaucrat on hold when 'We're back in 5!' — asking them to hold while he does live television
jokes.setup: Hank is mid-negotiation with a licensing bureaucrat about his alcohol permit when the floor director counts down to air
jokes.punchline: Hank asks the supervisor — after a passive-aggressive exchange — to hold, then walks back on air for a commercial segment, apparently planning to resume the fight afterward
jokes.explanation: Great cringe setup: Hank's inability to separate his restaurant obsession from his actual job. The passive-aggressive corporate-speak with the bureaucrat ('I would be absolutely delighted and honored to speak to your supervisor') followed by immediate on-air transition is tonally rich. Character integration is high.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: I don't think Anybody's gonna... Come to The grand opening. [Sobbing]

jokes.text: Hank, on air with Burt Reynolds, plugs the restaurant again — 'where you and your food go on an adventure' — and Burt muses about investing.
jokes.setup: Hank is again promoting Hank's Look-Around Cafe on air, this time with Burt Reynolds as guest.
jokes.punchline: Burt Reynolds — currently living in a guesthouse because he can't afford a house — muses about investing in a rotating restaurant, which the audience knows is an enterprise already showing signs of disaster.
jokes.explanation: The callback to Burt's financial situation makes this funnier than the surface joke. The irony of a broke movie star considering investing in a doomed restaurant is rich, though it requires the audience to connect the dots. The 'go on an adventure' tagline is also funny in its own desperate-PR way.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Even my own wife Is not coming Because there's, You know, 'Sorry, honey, there's A death in the family,'

jokes.text: Hank on air plugs his restaurant again — Burt Reynolds plays along, then undercuts it with 'Like Smokey and the Bandit. That was a great idea. And Cannonball Run. That was a great idea.' — delivered mockingly
jokes.setup: Hank is doing his second on-air restaurant plug; Burt appears to be playing along supportively
jokes.punchline: Burt sarcastically equates 'rotating restaurant' with his own notorious box office failures — 'Smokey and the Bandit' and 'Cannonball Run' — 'great ideas' all
jokes.explanation: Exceptional joke for insider comedy audiences. Burt Reynolds — the actual Burt Reynolds — name-dropping his own notoriously middlebrow films as examples of 'great ideas' as a way of insulting Hank's rotating restaurant is layered and self-aware. It works on multiple levels: it's Burt being self-deprecating, it's a genuine insult to Hank, and it's delivered with the cadence of false praise. Strong originality and character integration — only Burt Reynolds can make this joke.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: You drink water, Arthur. You drink Through your ass!

jokes.text: Hank laughs uncertainly at Burt's observation. Burt says 'No, it's a great idea, I'm telling you,' then lists it alongside Smokey and the Bandit and Cannonball Run — all his own movies — as 'great ideas.'
jokes.setup: Burt has just pointed out a problem with the restaurant and Hank is unsure if he's being mocked.
jokes.punchline: Burt reassures him the restaurant is a great idea, then compares it to Smokey and the Bandit and Cannonball Run — his own films, implicitly self-deprecating about their quality — creating an inadvertent insult inside a compliment.
jokes.explanation: Burt's celebrity self-deprecation, playing Smokey and Cannonball Run as questionable benchmarks for 'great ideas,' is a sharp piece of meta-celebrity comedy. Hank doesn't fully process that the comparison might not be flattering, which adds another layer.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: This fucking Electrical engineer! You know! This-- This-- this guy, He-- he comes in, He fills in at The last minute, And i-- I'm supposed to-- I'm supposed to think That this guy Knows fuck-all About anything!

jokes.text: Artie arrives again to find Hank sleeping at the office a second morning: 'You gotta stop sleeping here, Hank! It's beginning to smell like a goddamn locker room.'
jokes.setup: Artie arrives at work a second day to find Hank has again spent the night at the office
jokes.punchline: Artie's disgust is now escalated from surprised to exasperated — 'smell like a goddamn locker room' confirms this has become a pattern
jokes.explanation: Running gag payoff — the repeat of the sleeping-at-office joke works because Artie's complaint has escalated from 'what are you doing here' to sensory disgust. The locker room detail is specific and funny, but the joke is dependent on the callback for its impact.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Oh, shit, If I had a gun! If I had a gun, Artie!

jokes.text: Hank sarcastically commenting on Burt Reynolds: 'Give a guy a couple of car chases and all of a sudden he thinks he's an incredible wit.'
jokes.setup: Artie tells Hank that Burt Reynolds thinks Hank is a 'loose cannon' close to mental collapse
jokes.punchline: Hank dismisses Burt's assessment by reducing his entire career to 'a couple of car chases' — oblivious to the irony that Burt's assessment of him is entirely accurate
jokes.explanation: Hank's dismissal of Burt Reynolds — a massive movie star — as 'just a guy with car chases' while being a secondary talk show host is a rich irony. The callback to Burt's own self-deprecating car chase joke makes this land harder on rewatch.

dialogue.speaker: Phil
dialogue.line: He's telling me About his troubles At the restaurant. But you're Not in there. He doesn't know that.

jokes.text: Hank insists 'I am here. Hank Kingsley is present and accounted for' — then immediately runs off to make a restaurant phone call
jokes.setup: Artie begs Hank to focus on the show; Hank emphatically insists he's fully present
jokes.punchline: Mid-declaration of presence, he remembers an urgent restaurant call and runs off — the irony is immediate and complete
jokes.explanation: Textbook ironic self-defeat: the joke is in the instant contradiction of Hank's own words. 'Hank Kingsley is present and accounted for' functions as a formal declaration immediately followed by a total abdication. Well-structured; the formal third-person self-address before the collapse is a nice touch.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: well, he's been in the men's room for an hour now... vomiting and weeping.

jokes.text: Hank breaks down crying about the grand opening cancellations — 'Even my own wife is not coming because there's a death in the family'
jokes.setup: Hank confesses he's in real trouble — every RSVP is a cancellation, and he begins to genuinely cry
jokes.punchline: His wife's excuse is a 'death in the family' — the most legitimate possible reason not to attend — which Hank presents as part of a conspiracy against him
jokes.explanation: Dark comedy: Hank is so self-absorbed that a family death registers only as an inconvenient excuse. The comedy comes from the gap between the legitimate excuse and Hank's inability to accept any reason as legitimate. His genuine emotional distress makes this both funny and uncomfortable — which is the show's highest mode.

dialogue.line: Instead of Saying 'hank's Look-around cafe,' It says 'Look-round cafe.'

jokes.text: Hank, through tears, asks Artie 'You're gonna be there, aren't you, buddy?' — then a long pause before Artie's guilty response
jokes.setup: Hank is weeping and has just confessed that nobody is coming to his grand opening
jokes.punchline: He turns to Artie with desperate hope — the pause before Artie's answer (which confirms he also has plans) is the joke; the silence does the heavy lifting
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best moments — pure Larry Sanders Show. The comedy is entirely in the pause and what it implies. Artie — who we know has plans — must choose between honesty and kindness, and the silence tells us everything. Hank's vulnerability makes this genuinely moving AND funny simultaneously. The callback to Artie's earlier 'I've got plans' makes this devastating on rewatch. Near-perfect structure.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Ah, that's ok.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: It is?

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Mm-hmm.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: You sure? 'Cause I could try To go out and buy an 'a.'

jokes.text: Artie's guilty answer: 'Oh, damn it! Well, Hank, you've changed the grand opening so many times! I do have a life of my own, you know.'
jokes.setup: Artie has been caught by Hank's tearful plea; the pause broke and now Artie must confess
jokes.punchline: Artie — the one person Hank trusted — also has plans and defends himself with the same reasoning everyone else used, complete with exasperation
jokes.explanation: The payoff works because Artie's exasperation is totally justified (Hank HAS changed the date multiple times) even as Hank's devastation is also real. Both are right, which is the source of the dark comedy. 'I do have a life of my own' from Artie is a rare glimpse of his private self.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Won't last forever.

jokes.text: Hank's full paranoid breakdown listing enemies: wife, staff, 'the whole staff,' government, 'and uh... this fucking electrical engineer!'
jokes.setup: Hank is spiraling into a paranoid rant about who is 'against' him
jokes.punchline: The list escalates from plausible grievances (wife, staff) to increasingly abstract forces (government) before bottoming out with something hyper-specific and mundane ('this fucking electrical engineer!')
jokes.explanation: Excellent list comedy. The structure builds from intimate to grandiose (wife → government) and then collapses into the hyper-specific ('this fucking electrical engineer!') which is the comedic release. It's a perfect paranoid narcissist's list — the electrical engineer who installed the wrong motor is somehow the final enemy in a conspiracy that includes the US government. High originality in the specific endpoint.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: And it's called, uh-- Uh...

jokes.text: Hank, mid-meltdown speech about why people should support him, says 'You drink through your ass!' to Artie when offered water
jokes.setup: Artie is trying to calm Hank down: 'You gotta breathe. Breathe!' and offers him water
jokes.punchline: Hank, still in tears, rejects the water offer with 'You drink water, Arthur. You drink through your ass!' — a non sequitur insult that reveals his collapse while also being absurdly funny
jokes.explanation: An unexpected line that erupts from Hank's breakdown. 'You drink through your ass' makes no sense as an insult, which is what makes it so funny — it's pure emotional noise with the grammar of an insult. Tambor delivers it with the conviction of a real grievance. High quotability.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: I'm gonna take A long fuckin' walk.

jokes.text: Artie quietly slips out of the room while Hank continues his meltdown, leaving Hank talking to an empty room — then tells his assistant 'He doesn't know that.' when asked where Hank thinks Artie is
jokes.setup: Artie is 'listening' to Hank's meltdown while simultaneously making administrative decisions
jokes.punchline: Artie has exited the room entirely; Hank is still monologuing passionately to no one — confirmed by Artie's assistant asking 'but you're not in there' and Artie's reply 'He doesn't know that.'
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's standout moments. Artie's complete pragmatism — he's providing 'therapeutic' attention to Hank while simultaneously running the show from outside the room — captures his character perfectly. 'He doesn't know that' is a perfect deadpan punchline: four words that reveal both Artie's compassion (he didn't abandon Hank cruelly) and his efficiency (he's getting work done). High marks across all categories.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry Seinfeld
dialogue.line: Hey, is this How things usually Work around here?

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Yeah.

jokes.text: Artie: 'Get Dr. Landy on the phone.' Assistant: 'Who?' Artie: 'Dr. Eugene Landy. Our good friend Brian Wilson will have his number.'
jokes.setup: Having listened to Hank's complete psychological meltdown, Artie decides on a course of action
jokes.punchline: He calls for Brian Wilson's controversial therapist Dr. Eugene Landy — famous for his total psychological control over Wilson — which implies Hank needs not just help but full psychological management
jokes.explanation: Exceptional insider joke. Dr. Eugene Landy was Brian Wilson's real-life therapist/Svengali who became notorious for achieving total psychological dominance over his patient — a massive scandal in the music industry at the time. Artie calling for Landy implies Hank needs not therapy but complete psychological takeover, which is both a very dark joke and a very specific celebrity reference. High originality because it requires cultural knowledge to land fully, and when it does it's devastating. Among the episode's best.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry Seinfeld
dialogue.line: I wrote this, Uh, script For your show. Would this be a bad time To give it to you?

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Yeah! Yeah.

jokes.text: Artie's voicemail to Larry: 'Hank's not doing so well... he's been in the men's room for an hour now, vomiting and weeping.'
jokes.setup: Artie leaves Larry a voicemail updating him on the situation — Burt Reynolds quit, going to try Jerry Seinfeld next door
jokes.punchline: Buried at the end of the administrative update: Hank has been in the men's room for an hour, vomiting and weeping — delivered with the same flat affect as the scheduling news
jokes.explanation: The deadpan delivery of 'vomiting and weeping' as a casual addendum to logistical updates is a masterclass in the show's comedy style. The 'and' joining those two verbs is perfect — they're presented as equally unremarkable data points. This is the highest form of Larry Sanders Show humor: professional normalizing of human breakdown. Strong marks across all categories.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: If this fucking booth Starts to rotate, I swear to god...

jokes.text: Artie's message continues: 'Also, uh... well, Hank's not doing so well. He's been under quite a bit of pressure lately and seems a bit rattled.'
jokes.setup: Artie is updating Larry on Hank's condition, having just witnessed him scream 'If I had a gun!'
jokes.punchline: 'Seems a bit rattled' — after a scene of Hank threatening imaginary violence over a rotating floor and raving about the government — is a breathtaking understatement.
jokes.explanation: The gap between what we just witnessed (a full-scale breakdown including implied gun threats) and Artie's clinical 'seems a bit rattled' is enormous and perfectly deployed. This is deadpan understatement at its finest — a comedy technique that requires the audience to hold the full previous scene in mind. The callback structure is what makes it land so hard. Earns 8+.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: I'm gonna shove it Up Hank's ass If he ever gets here, The son of a bitch.

jokes.text: Artie informs Larry that Hank has been vomiting and weeping for an hour; Larry's response is 'How bad is Hank?' — not 'Is Hank okay?'
jokes.setup: Artie has relayed the graphic Hank update to Larry on vacation
jokes.punchline: Larry's question 'How bad is Hank?' treats Hank's breakdown as a managerial problem to be assessed rather than a human crisis to respond to — pure Larry Sanders self-preservation instinct
jokes.explanation: 'How bad is Hank?' instead of 'Is Hank okay?' is a subtle but precise character joke. The phrasing reveals Larry's relationship to other humans: they are variables to be calibrated, not people to be comforted. Maximum character integration with high economy — the joke lives in a single word difference.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry Seinfeld
dialogue.line: He's just weird.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: That's exactly What ours does.

jokes.text: Sign update: Instead of 'Hank's Look-Around Cafe,' the installed sign reads 'Look-Round Cafe' — missing the letter A. Hank's response: 'Ah, that's ok. See? It's great.'
jokes.setup: One final piece of bad news: the sign was installed wrong — missing the 'A' in 'Look-Around'
jokes.punchline: Rather than react with his usual explosion, Hank — now beyond breaking — simply accepts it. 'See? It's great.' The total psychological surrender is the punchline.
jokes.explanation: Excellent payoff to the escalation. After Hank's explosion about everything that's gone wrong, his complete acceptance of the wrong sign — 'See? It's great' — signals psychological collapse rather than genuine equanimity. The humor is dark: this is a man who has broken. The specific detail (missing 'A' from 'Look-Around') is concrete and funny on its own, and the absence of a meltdown is funnier than any meltdown could be at this point.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Yeah. It's 9:30 a.M. We looked for you All night, Hank. No!

jokes.text: Hank tries to get Jerry Seinfeld to call Hank's restaurant his 'après-comedy bistro of choice' using that exact wording. Jerry: 'No-o-o. No. [chuckles] Can't do that.'
jokes.setup: Hank offers to ask Jerry on air what he's doing this weekend — in exchange, Hank wants a scripted endorsement using specific promotional language
jokes.punchline: Jerry's amused but firm 'No-o-o. Can't do that.' — the extended vowel conveying mild disbelief at the ask — is a perfect celebrity reaction to a desperate pitch
jokes.explanation: Excellent cringe setup: Hank's 'après-comedy bistro of choice' is the most stilted possible promotional language — clearly drafted by someone who has watched too many TV ads. Seinfeld's refusal is pitch-perfect: not angry, just mildly incredulous and completely unbothered. The tension between Hank's desperation and Seinfeld's ease is the heart of the joke.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Make it go back. Make it go back. Turn back the world.

jokes.text: Hank warns Seinfeld: 'You know, they put you on Thursday nights, so you've got a little heat going for you right now. Won't last forever.'
jokes.setup: Seinfeld has politely declined Hank's promotional request; Hank tries one final angle
jokes.punchline: Hank — a sidekick — threatens Jerry Seinfeld's career longevity as leverage in a restaurant endorsement negotiation. The complete inversion of power is the joke.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best and most quotable lines. Hank Kingsley — a second banana talk show announcer — delivering a career-threat to Jerry Seinfeld over a restaurant endorsement he can't compel is perfectly calibrated absurdism. The line is delivered with complete sincerity, which makes it more devastating. The layered irony (Seinfeld's show was at its peak; Hank has no leverage whatsoever) rewards TV-history-savvy viewers enormously. High originality, high character integration, near-perfect economy. Comparable to the 8.0 anchor and arguably exceeds it.

jokes.text: Hank's warm-up: announces he's going to talk about his restaurant, then appears to forget the name of the restaurant mid-speech — whispers frantically
jokes.setup: Hank announces a 'very special warm-up' about his own restaurant
jokes.punchline: He can't remember the name of his own restaurant — the thing he's been obsessing over for the entire episode — and is reduced to frantic whispering, presumably to a crew member
jokes.explanation: Superb cringe payoff. After an entire episode of Hank's obsessive restaurant promotion, he blanks on the name in front of a live audience. The joke is both a perfect callback and a character revelation: the stress has finally consumed even the thing he was promoting. The visible whisper (inferred from stage direction) makes this a great physical moment. The audience laughter confirms the landing.

jokes.text: Hank, after the memory blank: '[Inhales] Guess we're not gonna have that, uh, special warm-up.'
jokes.setup: Hank has just forgotten his own restaurant's name in front of the audience.
jokes.punchline: His recovery: quietly abandoning the entire premise with maximum understatement — 'Guess we're not gonna have that, uh, special warm-up.' Then a deep breath. Then laughter from the audience.
jokes.explanation: The callback to 'very special warm-up' — now abandoned — is perfect. The economy of the line is excellent (Hank surrendering an entire planned bit in one gentle sentence), and the inhale before it tells us how much effort the surrender takes. Strong deadpan understatement.

jokes.text: Hank: 'I'm gonna take a long fuckin' walk.' [Microphone thuds] [Silence]
jokes.setup: After forgetting his restaurant's name during the warm-up, Hank collects himself — then announces he's leaving
jokes.punchline: He drops the microphone and walks off stage in front of the live audience — the mic thud and then silence is the punchline; the audience silence afterward amplifies the absurdity
jokes.explanation: The episode's comedic peak. 'I'm gonna take a long fuckin' walk' followed by a mic drop in front of a live studio audience is the perfect culmination of Hank's entire arc this episode. The language (one word, perfectly chosen), the gesture (mic drop before mic drops were cultural), and the silence that follows constitute a fully staged comedic moment that requires no dialogue. The four words and sound effects do everything. Maximum economy, structure, and character integration. This is what the whole episode has been building to.

jokes.text: Jerry Seinfeld and Larry watch Hank walk off: 'Is this how things usually work around here?' Larry: 'Yeah.'
jokes.setup: Seinfeld has just watched Hank abandon the warm-up mid-sentence and walk off the lot
jokes.punchline: Larry's 'Yeah' — utterly unfazed — confirms that Hank walking off is within normal operating parameters for this show
jokes.explanation: Classic Larry Sanders straight-man delivery. The 'Yeah' normalizes the chaos and functions as both character reveal (Larry's blasé adaptation to crisis) and meta-commentary on the show's world. Seinfeld's setup question is functional; Larry's single-word confirmation is the joke.

jokes.text: A writer tries to hand Larry a script he wrote for the show — 'Would this be a bad time to give it to you?' — Larry: 'Yeah.' — 'Oh. OK.' — [leaves]
jokes.setup: In the midst of the post-Hank chaos, a writer (presumably an intern or staff writer) tries to pitch a script
jokes.punchline: Larry's 'Yeah' again — now explicitly confirming a bad time — and the writer's uncomplaining 'Oh. OK.' and exit is a miniature comedy of workplace social ineptitude
jokes.explanation: Functional background joke about workplace tone-deafness. The bit is light but earns its place — the 'Yeah' callback from the previous joke creates a brief rhythm. Not a strong standalone but contributes to the episode's texture.

jokes.text: Larry and Artie at the grand opening: Artie threatens to shove the ice sculpture of the Queen Mary 'up Hank's ass if he ever gets here'
jokes.setup: Larry and Artie have abandoned their plans and shown up at Hank's grand opening — but Hank is missing
jokes.punchline: Artie's affection for Hank is expressed as a violent threat involving a buffet ice sculpture — the specific detail (Queen Mary) is absurdist and precise
jokes.explanation: Rip Torn's Artie expressing love through violent imagery is a character signature. The ice sculpture of the Queen Mary is a specific, absurdist detail that elevates the threat from generic profanity to something genuinely funny. The fact that both Larry and Artie have broken their own plans to show up for Hank makes this moment warm underneath the profanity.

jokes.text: Larry: 'I just can't believe I took the time out of my vacation to come here, and the man isn't even here.'
jokes.setup: Larry and Artie are at the grand opening, which Hank is missing.
jokes.punchline: Larry, who has been on vacation and is the nominal star of the show (not the restaurant owner), is now at the restaurant he was dragged to — and Hank isn't there. The irony of the only person who had legitimate reasons not to attend being the one who showed up.
jokes.explanation: Good irony — Larry, the one person with a legitimate excuse (vacation), is at the opening, and Hank isn't. The character work is solid. Not a standout joke but a good structural beat.

jokes.text: Larry complains he 'can't believe I took time out of my vacation to come here, and the man isn't even here' — while Artie says 'I'm already seasick' from the rotating floor
jokes.setup: Larry and Artie are sitting in a rotating booth at Hank's grand opening
jokes.punchline: The rotating floor that has been a running gag all episode is now literally making Artie seasick — confirming the absurdity of Hank's restaurant concept via physical discomfort
jokes.explanation: Perfect running gag payoff: Mull's centrifugal force joke, the motor problems, the bearing rust — all of it has led to Artie literally getting seasick from the floor. Larry's paranoid 'this booth doesn't rotate, does it?' followed by 'If this fucking booth starts to rotate I swear to god' is also great character work. Both jokes land because the setup has been consistent all episode.

jokes.text: Larry: 'If this fucking booth starts to rotate, I swear to god...' — trail off
jokes.setup: Larry is sitting in a rotating restaurant booth and has just been told Artie is seasick
jokes.punchline: His unfinished threat trails off — he doesn't even know what he'd do, which captures his helplessness and anxiety perfectly
jokes.explanation: Larry's unfinished threats are a character signature — he escalates to profanity and then has no follow-through because he fundamentally can't control anything. The trailing 'I swear to god' with no conclusion is both funny and true to the character.

jokes.text: Larry and Artie discover Hank was found asleep on an empty stage by 'the weird intern' — Seinfeld: 'We got one of those.' Larry: 'What's yours do?' Seinfeld: 'He's just weird. That's exactly what ours does.'
jokes.setup: Seinfeld mentions he sent 'the weird intern' to find Hank on the empty stage
jokes.punchline: Larry's 'What's yours do?' and Seinfeld's 'He's just weird. That's exactly what ours does.' — the universality of the useless weird intern is the observation
jokes.explanation: Beautifully economical observational bit. 'He's just weird. That's exactly what ours does.' is the kind of joke that rewards the specific phrasing — the question 'What's yours do?' implies job function; the answer 'He's just weird' confirms the intern's only function is ambient weirdness. Highly quotable for the precise echo structure ('That's exactly what ours does'). Strong economy.

jokes.text: Seinfeld hands off passed-out Hank to Larry and Artie: 'I'll send you a bill for the drool.'
jokes.setup: Seinfeld has found Hank asleep/passed out on the stage and is returning him to Larry and Artie
jokes.punchline: 'I'll send you a bill for the drool' — treating Hank's unconscious state as a minor service rendered and billing for biological damage
jokes.explanation: Sharp exit line. 'The drool' is a great specific detail that implies the visual without describing it. The joke treats Hank's breakdown as a transaction rather than a crisis, which is both funny and Seinfeld-appropriate (his stand-up observations often find the transactional in the emotional). High economy.

jokes.text: Artie tells the groggy Hank: 'It's 9:30 A.M. We looked for you all night, Hank.' — Hank's response: 'No!'
jokes.setup: Hank wakes up thinking it's 9:30 PM and he can still make it to his grand opening
jokes.punchline: It's 9:30 AM — the grand opening was last night and Hank slept through it — his one-word 'No!' is the comedic devastation
jokes.explanation: The episode's ultimate payoff. The entire episode has been about Hank's desperate attempts to get people to his grand opening — and Hank slept through it himself. The structure is flawless: the misdirection (we think it's 9:30 PM), the correction (9:30 AM), and Hank's one-word response. 'No!' is all you need. High structure and economy. One of the episode's genuinely great comic beats.

jokes.text: Hank: 'Make it go back. Make it go back. Turn back the world.'
jokes.setup: Hank has just been told he missed his own grand opening by sleeping through it
jokes.punchline: His response is a delirious, poetic request for time reversal — 'Turn back the world' — which is both genuinely sad and completely absurd
jokes.explanation: A surprisingly poetic punchline. 'Make it go back. Make it go back. Turn back the world.' shifts from repetitive panic to sudden grandeur — 'Turn back the world' is almost Shakespearean in its scale of despair, which makes it both absurd and genuine. Tambor's delivery (implied from the phrasing) would make this devastating. Among the most quotable lines in the episode.

jokes.text: Larry's closing complaint: 'Hey, you know, I was up all night. I'm supposed to be on vacation. My wife wants to go to Vegas...'
jokes.setup: Hank has just had his grand opening dream destroyed; Larry and Artie have been up all night
jokes.punchline: Larry immediately pivots to his own inconvenience — Vegas trip delayed — as Hank processes his catastrophe, capturing Larry's essential self-involvement perfectly
jokes.explanation: The perfect coda. Larry's inability to sit with anyone else's pain — pivoting immediately to his Vegas trip while Hank grieves — is the best possible last line. It recalibrates the episode's emotional register back to comedy and confirms that nothing has changed or will change. Strong character integration.

tmdb_overview: Larry goes on vacation, but the problems follow him as Hank alienates a series of co-hosts as he anxiously awaits the opening night of Hank's Lookaround Restaurant.
